claims.text: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi nanoparticles have a critical particle size governing structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K.
Particles smaller than the critical size have enhanced atomic mobility.
Particles smaller than the critical size develop local compositional fluctuations that lead to early phase segregation.
Larger AlCoCrFeNi nanoparticles maintain a stable, single-phase solid solution.
Surface-to-volume ratio and nanoscale compositional fluctuations govern size-dependent atomic mobility.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface energy and larger surface-to-volume ratios than larger nanoparticles.
Higher surface energy and surface-to-volume ratio accelerate atomic diffusion in smaller AlCoCrFeNi nanoparticles.
Accelerated diffusion enhances local compositional fluctuations and facilitates phase segregation or ordering at lower temperatures.
Reduced surface-driven diffusion allows larger nanoparticles to preserve single-phase stability at high temperature.
The critical particle-size threshold is likely approximately 10 nm or less.
Particles at or below approximately 10 nm will show earlier phase segregation or secondary-phase formation as temperature increases.
Approximately 20 nm particles will retain a homogeneous single-phase structure throughout 473–1923 K under the specified conditions.
Phase segregation or secondary-phase formation will be observable through lattice-parameter shifts, emergent diffraction peaks, TEM contrast, or compositional mapping.

The proposed size-dependent behavior is expected to hold under inert atmospheres and controlled heating but may deviate under oxidizing conditions or when particle shape or composition is initially heterogeneous.
